claims.text: Cold spray deposition of a tailored Ni-based repair alloy followed by low-temperature annealing can repair a localized damaged surface.
The proposed repair will avoid the hot cracking associated with traditional fusion-welding repair.
Traditional fusion processing presents a hot-cracking risk for the proposed class of high-performance superalloys or corrosion-resistant stainless steels.
Annealing at approximately 400–500 °C in argon will induce diffusion bonding at the repair–substrate interface.
Annealing at approximately 400–500 °C will promote microstructural homogenization at the interface.
The proposed process will form a dense, gradient microstructure at the repair–substrate interface.
The low heat input of cold spray will preserve the substrate's integrity.
A diffusion-bonded repair layer will enhance surface hardness.
A diffusion-bonded repair layer will reduce crack-initiation sites.
Cold spray deposits the repair alloy in the solid state without melting.
Avoiding melting avoids the thermal stresses associated with fusion processing.
Low-temperature annealing facilitates atomic interdiffusion across the repair–substrate interface.
The combined cold-spray and annealing process minimizes residual stresses and refines the microstructural transition.
Minimizing residual stress and refining the interfacial transition will delay or prevent surface-defect initiation in aggressive environments.
The repaired surface will have greater hardness than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The repaired surface will have better corrosion resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The repaired surface will have better wear resistance than both a fusion-welded repair and an untreated surface.
The repaired surface will have a lower tendency for hot cracking than a traditional fusion-welded repair.
The intervention is limited to localized repairs for which cold spray can be adequately controlled and the repair alloy is compatible with the substrate.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis compares hot-cracking tendency against an untreated surface and describes untreated surfaces as prone to hot cracking, although hot cracking is elsewhere presented as a consequence of fusion processing; an untreated surface has not undergone that process.
